patient.name: Yetunde Bello
patient.complaint: Two weeks of brief spinning attacks when she rolls over in bed or looks up
background: Bad cold with a cough 3 weeks ago
Osteopenia on calcium and vitamin D
Pharmacist in Croydon; lives with her husband

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with vertigo lasting seconds, triggered by head movement, with no hearing loss: the duration, the trigger and the ears separate BPPV from vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis and Ménière's.

points: Yetunde, 58: the room **spins** when she **rolls onto her right side** in bed.
Also when she **looks up** to a high shelf.
Each attack lasts about **20 seconds**, then settles.
Nauseated; no hearing change, tinnitus or ear fullness.

steps.lead: Brief spins brought on by **head position**: a peripheral (inner ear) problem where loose **otoconia** send false rotation signals.
Yetunde had a **viral illness** 3 weeks ago, a recognised association; head trauma is the other.

visual.title: How long does each attack last?
visual.label: Yetunde ~20 s
visual.caption: Seconds = BPPV. Minutes to hours = Ménière's or vestibular migraine. Continuous for days = vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis.

steps.lead: Yetunde's attacks are **under 30 seconds**, set off by rolling in bed and looking up, with **no hearing loss** and no neurological deficit.

points: Cranial nerves, limbs and gait normal.
No nystagmus at rest; ears and drums normal.

steps.lead: Yetunde has **no red flags**: no headache, diplopia, weakness or ataxia. Any of those would point to a **central** cause such as cerebellar stroke.

steps.q: Which bedside test should the GP do next?
steps.r: The **Dix-Hallpike** reproduces the vertigo and shows the nystagmus. Epley is the treatment, not the test.

steps.lead: Turned to the right and lowered, Yetunde spins after a short delay with **torsional nystagmus** towards the **right (affected) ear**.
Yetunde has osteopenia, so a **fall** during a sudden attack is her biggest risk.

steps.text: Vertigo after a cold is not automatically vestibular neuritis. Neuritis is **continuous for days**; Yetunde's spins last **seconds** and need a head movement.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?': the answer is the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre, not imaging or audiometry, unless the stem gives central red flags.

steps.title: Dix-Hallpike (right side)
nodes: Lie back quickly, head hanging 20° below the couch
Watch the eyes for 30 to 60 seconds
steps.caption: The ear that is lowest when symptoms start is the affected ear.

visual.title: What a positive test looks like over time
visual.label: Yetunde: starts at ~4 s
visual.caption: A brief latency, then torsional nystagmus that fades within a minute: a peripheral pattern.

steps.lead: Yetunde's **right Dix-Hallpike** is positive: this clinical test is the **gold standard**, and no scan is needed.

steps.q: Which Dix-Hallpike feature would make you worry about a central cause instead?
o: A few seconds' latency before nystagmus
Nystagmus that fades within a minute
Pure downbeating nystagmus with no latency that does not fatigue
Torsional nystagmus towards the lower ear
steps.r: **No latency, no fatigue, pure vertical** nystagmus suggests a central lesion. Yetunde's latency, torsion and fatigue are classic BPPV.

steps.text: Do not order an MRI or CT for typical BPPV. Imaging is only for **red flags**: headache, diplopia, ataxia, weakness or atypical nystagmus.
BPPV is a **clinical** diagnosis: history (seconds, positional, no hearing loss) plus a positive Dix-Hallpike. Audiometry is normal.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' after a positive Dix-Hallpike: the Epley manoeuvre. Brandt-Daroff exercises are for home, and prochlorperazine only briefly for nausea.

steps.q: Yetunde's right Dix-Hallpike is positive. What is the most appropriate management?
steps.r: **Epley** repositions the otoconia and treats the cause. Betahistine is for Ménière's; prochlorperazine only eases nausea.

steps.lead: The GP performs an **Epley manoeuvre** on Yetunde's right side in the same appointment.

steps.title: Epley manoeuvre (right ear)
nodes: Start as a right Dix-Hallpike: head 45° right, lie back
Roll onto left side, nose to the floor
steps.caption: Hold each position about 30 seconds or until the vertigo stops.

steps.lead: Yetunde is taught **Brandt-Daroff exercises** for home and given a few days of **prochlorperazine** for nausea only.

visual.title: Yetunde's attacks after Epley
visual.caption: Most patients improve quickly after one or two Epley manoeuvres.

steps.lead: If Yetunde's spins come back, the manoeuvre is **repeated**, or she is referred for **vestibular rehabilitation**.
Yetunde's care follows **NICE CKS** on vertigo: Epley first, home exercises, avoid long-term vestibular sedatives, review if not improving.

steps.text: Vestibular sedatives (prochlorperazine, cinnarizine) do **not** treat BPPV and slow central compensation. Use them briefly, for nausea only.
Safety-net Yetunde: get up slowly, sit on the bed edge first, and take care on stairs. **Falls** are the main harm.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: which canal is involved and why (posterior, the most dependent), why head movement triggers it, and how the Epley manoeuvre works.

steps.lead: Yetunde's otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) have broken loose from the **utricle** and fallen into her right **posterior** canal, the lowest one when she lies down.

steps.title: Why rolling over makes the room spin
nodes: Loose otoconia in the posterior canal
Head moves into the plane of that canal
Crystals fall with gravity through endolymph
False rotation signal → vertigo and nystagmus

steps.lead: When Yetunde rolls over, the crystals move through the **endolymph** and bend the **cupula**, so her brain gets a spin signal her eyes do not match.

o: The cochlea compensates for vestibular loss
The problem is mechanical debris in a semicircular canal
The lesion is in the brainstem
steps.r: BPPV is **loose debris** in a canal: the cochlea and nerves are untouched. Labyrinthitis inflames the whole labyrinth, so hearing is lost.

steps.lead: Yetunde's problem is **purely mechanical** canal debris, so there is no hearing loss and no brainstem or cerebellar sign.
Each Epley position uses **gravity** to roll Yetunde's crystals round the canal and back into the **utricle**, where they no longer stimulate the cupula.

mcq.q: How long do BPPV vertigo episodes typically last?
mcq.r: BPPV attacks are **brief (<30 s)** and positional. Hours suggests Ménière's; days suggests neuritis.
BPPV is associated with **recent viral illness or head trauma**.

mcq.q: Which feature is NOT expected in BPPV?
mcq.r: BPPV has **no hearing loss** and no focal neurological deficit.

mcq.q: Which feature suggests a central cause rather than BPPV?
mcq.r: **Diplopia**, ataxia, weakness or severe headache are red flags for a central cause such as cerebellar stroke.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard test for BPPV?
mcq.r: The **Dix-Hallpike** reproduces vertigo with torsional nystagmus after brief latency.

mcq.q: What does a positive Dix-Hallpike show?
o: Reproduced vertigo with torsional nystagmus after a brief latency
mcq.r: **Latency, torsional nystagmus and reproduced vertigo** are the classic positive result.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for BPPV?
Which exercises can patients do at home for BPPV?
Which semicircular canal is most often affected in BPPV?
mcq.r: The **posterior** canal is most dependent, so otoconia settle there.

mcq.q: Where do the otoconia in BPPV come from?

practice.stem: An 81 year old woman has fallen twice in a week. Both falls happened when she reached up to hang washing, and she felt the room spin for a few seconds. She has no chest pain, palpitations or loss of consciousness. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular, lying BP 138/80 mmHg and standing BP 134/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her falls?
practice.e: Brief spinning on looking up, without syncope, with normal postural BP and pulse, is BPPV; falls are its main complication in older people.

no chest pain, palpitations or loss of consciousness
steps.x: Neck extension triggers **spinning**, no syncope, no postural drop.

elim: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity causes syncope on neck turning or tight collars, not spinning.
No postural drop in BP.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man hit his head on a car door frame 10 days ago with no loss of consciousness. Since then he has had episodes of spinning lasting 10 to 15 seconds when he bends down or lies back. Hearing is normal. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Cranial nerve and cerebellar examination are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Head trauma is a recognised cause of BPPV: brief positional vertigo with normal hearing and neurology. A subdural would give headache and confusion.

steps.x: Trauma dislodges otoconia: brief positional vertigo.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Subdural: headache, confusion, fluctuating consciousness.
Perilymph fistula gives hearing loss and vertigo with straining.
Post-concussion gives headache and poor concentration, not brief positional spins.
Dissection: neck pain and posterior circulation signs.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman has brief vertigo when she rolls onto her left side in bed. On the left Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre, after a 4 second delay, she develops vertigo with torsional nystagmus beating towards the floor, which fades within 30 seconds. The right Dix-Hallpike is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

Vestibular nerve disease gives continuous vertigo.
Horizontal canal gives horizontal nystagmus on the supine roll test, and the right side is normal.
The right Dix-Hallpike is normal.

steps.x: **B. Left posterior canal.** The lower ear on a positive test is the affected one.

glossary.BPPV: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: brief vertigo from loose inner ear crystals, triggered by head movement.
glossary.Vertigo: A false sense that you or the room is spinning.
glossary.Otoconia: Tiny calcium carbonate crystals in the utricle that sense gravity and linear movement.
glossary.Utricle: An inner ear sac whose macula holds the otoconia.
glossary.Macula: The sensory patch in the utricle or saccule where otoconia sit.
glossary.Semicircular canal: One of three fluid-filled loops in the inner ear that sense head rotation.
glossary.Posterior canal: The most dependent semicircular canal; affected in most BPPV.
glossary.Endolymph: The fluid inside the semicircular canals.
glossary.Cupula: A jelly-like flap in each canal that bends with fluid movement to signal rotation.
glossary.Nystagmus: Involuntary rhythmic eye movements, with a slow drift and a fast corrective beat.
glossary.Torsional nystagmus: Nystagmus that rotates the eye around its front-to-back axis; typical of posterior canal BPPV.
glossary.Latency: The short delay of a few seconds before nystagmus starts on Dix-Hallpike.
glossary.Dix-Hallpike: A test that turns the head 45° and lies the patient back quickly to provoke BPPV.
glossary.Epley manoeuvre: A series of head positions that uses gravity to move otoconia back into the utricle.
glossary.Brandt-Daroff: Home exercises of repeated side-lying to settle BPPV.
glossary.Prochlorperazine: A dopamine antagonist used short-term for nausea and vertigo; it does not treat BPPV.
glossary.Vestibular sedatives: Drugs such as prochlorperazine and cinnarizine that dampen vertigo but slow recovery if used long-term.
glossary.Betahistine: A drug used in Ménière's disease to reduce attack frequency.
glossary.Vestibular rehabilitation: Exercise therapy that helps the brain compensate for vestibular problems.
glossary.Vestibular neuritis: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve: continuous vertigo for days, hearing normal.
glossary.Labyrinthitis: Inflammation of the labyrinth: continuous vertigo with hearing loss.
glossary.Ménière's disease: Endolymphatic hydrops causing attacks of vertigo for hours with tinnitus, fullness and hearing loss.
glossary.Endolymphatic hydrops: Excess endolymph in the inner ear, the mechanism of Ménière's disease.
glossary.Peripheral vertigo: Vertigo from the inner ear or vestibular nerve rather than the brain.
glossary.Central vertigo: Vertigo from the brainstem or cerebellum, e.g. stroke; often with neurological signs.
glossary.Cerebellar stroke: Infarction of the cerebellum; a dangerous central cause of vertigo with ataxia.
glossary.Diplopia: Double vision; a red flag in vertigo.
glossary.Dysdiadochokinesia: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements; a cerebellar sign.
glossary.Head impulse test: A bedside test for vestibular nerve function in continuous vertigo.
glossary.Romberg test: Standing with eyes shut to test position sense and balance.
glossary.Tinnitus: Ringing or buzzing in the ears.
glossary.Aural fullness: A feeling of pressure in the ear, typical of Ménière's disease.
glossary.Audiometry: Formal hearing test; normal in BPPV.
glossary.Rinne: Tuning fork test comparing air and bone conduction.
glossary.Weber: Tuning fork test placed on the forehead to lateralise hearing loss.
